nameStory: Dictyosphaerium gets its scientific name from Greek words meaning 'net sphere,' describing how these tiny algae cells arrange themselves in beautiful, mesh-like spherical colonies that look like microscopic soccer balls. The species name honors Christian Gottfried Ehrenberg, a 19th-century German naturalist who was one of the first scientists to study and describe these miniature aquatic organisms.
description: **Note: This is a microscopic freshwater algae, not a typical plant that can be seen with the naked eye.** Dictyosphaerium ehrenbergianum is a colonial green algae that forms tiny, hollow spherical clusters of cells connected by thin strands, creating a net-like appearance. Each colony is only about 20-200 micrometers across (smaller than the width of a human hair), so you'd need a microscope to observe its intricate structure. The individual cells within each colony are small and green, containing chlorophyll for photosynthesis.

idTips.label: Microscopic Structure
idTips.description: Requires microscope observation - appears as hollow, spherical colonies with cells connected by thin, thread-like strands forming a net pattern

idTips.label: Colony Shape
idTips.description: Forms perfectly round, ball-like clusters that maintain their spherical shape even when gently disturbed under the microscope

idTips.label: Cell Arrangement
idTips.description: Individual cells are positioned at the intersections of the net-like framework, giving the colony a geometric, almost crystalline appearance

idTips.label: Size Range
idTips.description: Colonies measure 20-200 micrometers in diameter - visible only under microscopic magnification, appearing as tiny green specks to the naked eye

idTips.label: Water Sample Appearance
idTips.description: In pond water samples, may contribute to a slight greenish tint or cloudiness, though individual colonies are invisible without magnification

habitat: Found in quiet freshwater environments like ponds, slow-moving streams, and shallow lake margins throughout New England. Prefers nutrient-rich waters with moderate temperatures and tends to be more abundant in areas with some organic matter but not heavily polluted conditions.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin to grow as water temperatures warm and daylight hours increase, making this a good time to find them in pond samples.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm months when optimal conditions support rapid colony reproduction and growth.
seasonality.fall: Still present but populations may decline as temperatures cool and daylight hours decrease, though some colonies persist.
seasonality.winter: Greatly reduced or absent in frozen waters, though may survive in deeper, unfrozen portions of water bodies.

funFact: Each spherical colony acts like a tiny living snow globe - the cells can actually move within their net-like framework, rotating and repositioning themselves to optimize light capture for photosynthesis, creating a mesmerizing dance visible only under a microscope.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other colonial green algae like Pediastrum, but Dictyosphaerium's distinctive hollow spherical shape and net-like cell arrangement set it apart from the flat, disc-like colonies of Pediastrum. Remember: Dictyosphaerium is a 3D sphere, Pediastrum is a flat disc.
contextualKnowledge: This organism represents the incredible microscopic diversity that exists in every drop of pond water - while we often think of New England's plant life in terms of trees and flowers, countless species of algae like this one form the invisible foundation of aquatic food webs.
